issues.subcategory: non-independence of dyadic data
issues.description: Participants are run and tested in pairs that jointly watch the movie and discuss the critical details, making the two members of each pair non-independent observations. The power analysis treats N=240 as the analytic sample and the planned two-factor ANOVA treats individuals as independent units. Dyadic dependence inflates Type I error and overstates effective power; the analysis should model pair as a clustering variable (e.g., multilevel model) or use the pair as the unit. This is not addressed anywhere.
issues.quote: The sample size will be set at 240 people (120 pairs).

issues.subcategory: contradictory counterbalancing vs. fixed discussed items
issues.description: The Design section states that discussed and non-discussed items are fully counterbalanced, but the Procedure states that every pair discusses the same fixed set of four critical details. If the same four items are always 'discussed' and the same four always 'non-discussed,' then discussion status is completely confounded with item identity, so any discussed/non-discussed difference could be an item effect rather than a misinformation effect. The two statements are mutually exclusive.
issues.quote: In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase. For example, all pairs will talk about Eric’s cap color and his company logo.

issues.subcategory: open-ended vs. forced-choice test format contradiction
issues.description: The Procedure and Analysis sections describe the individual memory test as containing 20 open-ended questions, but the Analysis plan elsewhere states the individual memory test will use a two-alternative forced-choice format. These are incompatible response formats with very different scoring and psychometric properties, and the discrepancy makes it impossible to know how the primary outcome will actually be measured or scored.
issues.quote: In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

issues.subcategory: intervention timing contradicts itself and the procedure
issues.description: The manuscript states in one place that the interventions/warning are placed AFTER the collaborative recall, and in another that the methods are placed BEFORE the collaborative recall to 'inoculate participants before misinformation could take effect.' The actual Procedure places the interventions as Phase 3, after collaborative recall (Phase 2). The 'before collaborative recall' justification directly contradicts the stated design and undermines the inoculation rationale.
issues.quote: What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation). The main reason for that is that we wanted to inoculate participants against the influence of misinformation before it could take effect.

issues.subcategory: inoculation framework misapplied to post-exposure timing
issues.description: The Demonstration and motivation method is grounded in McGuire's inoculation theory and Sagarin et al., both of which require that resistance be induced BEFORE the persuasive attack. In this design the intervention is delivered after the collaborative recall (after misinformation exposure). Applying an inoculation framework to a post-exposure manipulation is a conceptual mismatch that weakens the predicted mechanism.
issues.quote: This was inspired by existing research on resisting social influence presented by Sagarin, Cialdini, Rice, & Serna (2002). Their technique was based on the inoculation theory, introduced by McGuire (1964).

issues.subcategory: key moderator (awareness of discrepancies) never operationalized
issues.description: The central theoretical claim is that the methods will work only/more strongly for participants who are aware of discrepancies between their own memory and the co-witness misinformation. However, no procedure is described for measuring which participants are aware of the discrepancies (e.g., a source-monitoring or discrepancy-detection test). Without measuring awareness, the manuscript's core moderating hypothesis cannot be tested.
issues.quote: Thus, we expect that effectiveness of our methods will be higher among people aware of discrepancies between the original information and misinformation than among those unaware of such discrepancies.

issues.subcategory: unstable effect-size synthesis from heterogeneous studies
issues.description: The replication power analysis pools two studies with extremely heterogeneous effect sizes (Hedges' g = 1.92 vs. 0.38) into a single random-effects estimate of 1.13. With only two studies and such heterogeneity, the pooled estimate is unstable and not a defensible basis for power; the resulting required N of 18 is implausibly small and the synthesized value masks the true uncertainty.
issues.quote: Given the rather large difference in effect sizes between both studies, random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13.

issues.subcategory: implausibly low repeated-measures correlation drives power
issues.description: A correlation of r = 0.07 between discussed and non-discussed items is assumed for all repeated-measures power calculations. Such a low within-subject correlation is unusual and strongly influences the required sample size for within-between interactions. If the true correlation is higher or lower, the power calculations (and the claim of 'excellent power' for medium effects) could be substantially off. The choice is not justified beyond citing two studies, one of which had a very different effect.
issues.quote: A correlation r = 0.07 between repeated measures was assumed based on the research described above (Ito et al., 2019; Kękuś et al., 2020).

issues.subcategory: interventions confounded with format/engagement and time-on-task
issues.description: Three interventions are not matched on modality or duration: Extended warning and Education are ~7-minute passive podcasts, while Demonstration and motivation adds an active DRM task plus a motivational podcast (necessarily longer and more engaging), and the control is a soft-skills podcast. Any superiority of Demonstration could reflect the active task, greater duration, or arousal rather than its specific content, making the comparison confounded.
issues.quote: the motivational aspect will be achieved by a podcast (i.e., only with sound; no visual material will be included) explaining how harmful a situation is in which one witness reports details that they do not actually remember but which were heard from other witnesses.

issues.subcategory: no experimenter blinding
issues.description: The experimenter administers the interventions (including delivering DRM feedback and motivational instructions) and presumably scores some responses, but no blinding of experimenters to condition or to hypotheses is described. Given the demand-laden manipulations (telling participants 'you were fooled,' urging reliance on own memory), lack of blinding raises risk of experimenter expectancy effects.
issues.quote: At this moment in this group, the experimenter will give the following information to the participants: “Thank you for completing this memory task. Please take a look at your sheets now.

issues.subcategory: overclaim that normative influence is 'completely ruled out'
issues.description: The claim that normative impact is 'completely ruled out' because the final test is individual is too strong. Normative pressure during the collaborative discussion can produce agreement and re-encoding that persists into the private test, and social influence at encoding/consolidation is not eliminated merely because the test is private. Overstating this removes an important alternative explanation.
issues.quote: we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.

issues.subcategory: multiple outcome indices without correction
issues.description: Four separate indices (correct, misinformation-consistent, other, total answers) plus additional accuracy comparisons (filler, discussed, non-discussed) will all be analyzed with ANOVA, but no multiple-comparison correction or designation of a single primary outcome is specified. This creates undisclosed flexibility in which index 'counts' as supporting the hypotheses.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test’s scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.

issues.subcategory: directional (one-tailed) tests pre-specified
issues.description: Directional significance tests are assumed for the group comparisons, which roughly doubles power relative to two-tailed tests but is only appropriate if effects in the opposite direction would be treated as null. Given the authors themselves note that the interventions could plausibly increase conformity (e.g., reduced confidence), one-tailed testing may be inappropriate and inflates Type I error for the favored direction.
issues.quote: Comparisons among all groups and directional significance tests are assumed.

issues.subcategory: classifying all discussed items as 'misinformation' regardless of actual exposure
issues.description: All discussed items are categorized as containing misinformation, assuming the procedure exposed each participant to a conflicting co-witness version. However, partners may have guessed, agreed with the correct detail, or not actually voiced the conflicting detail. Without verifying from the audio that conflicting information was actually delivered to each participant on each item, this scoring misclassifies exposure and biases the misinformation index.
issues.quote: we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner’s differing version of events.

issues.subcategory: DRM feedback assumes the manipulation succeeded
issues.description: The Demonstration manipulation depends on participants having falsely recalled the critical lures, but the scripted feedback flatly tells participants 'If so, you were fooled' using fixed lure words. If a participant did not produce the lures, the demonstration of personal vulnerability fails for them, yet no contingency or check on per-participant manipulation success is described. This undermines the manipulation's intended mechanism for an unknown subset of participants.
issues.quote: See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief. If so, you were fooled.

issues.subcategory: vague exclusion rule and no dyad-level handling
issues.description: The only stated exclusion is 'technical problems,' which is undefined and open to interpretation. Critically, because data are dyadic, the manuscript does not specify what happens to the partner when one member of a pair is excluded, how missing/incomplete data will be handled, or whether excluded pairs will be replaced. This leaves room for undisclosed flexibility and unbalanced cells.
issues.quote: We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

issues.subcategory: hypothesis-awareness measured but no exclusion/handling rule
issues.description: Participants are asked to guess the study's true purpose and these responses are reserved for 'exploratory analysis,' but no a priori rule is given for whether suspicious participants (who detect the deception/MORI duality) will be excluded or how their awareness will be incorporated. Detection of the dual-movie manipulation could directly drive responses, and leaving handling unspecified introduces post hoc flexibility.
issues.quote: Next, the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.

issues.subcategory: convenience sample and narrow age range
issues.description: The sample is a self-selected, media/internet-recruited Polish convenience sample aged 16–35, yet the framing repeatedly extrapolates to real eyewitnesses and 'justice systems.' The restricted age band, single-country lab sample, and artificial MORI procedure limit generalization to actual forensic witnesses, but these limitations are not acknowledged as constraints on the conclusions.
issues.quote: The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.

issues.subcategory: power claim ignores dyadic clustering and planned-comparison N
issues.description: The conclusion that 240 participants gives 'excellent power' for medium effects relies on independence and on planned-comparison requirements (e.g., 82 for a medium effect). With 60 participants per group (effectively 30 pairs per group as independent units), the effective sample for between-group comparisons is far smaller than assumed, so the power claim is likely overstated for the key interaction and follow-up comparisons.
issues.quote: Considering the accessible financial, organizational and time resources, a sample of 240 participants was assumed; this allows for excellent power to detect medium and large effect sizes but not small ones.

issues.subcategory: certainty ratings collected but no analysis plan
issues.description: Subjective certainty ratings (0–100%) are collected for every answer, which are directly relevant to the manuscript's confidence-based theoretical claims (that people give wrong answers due to low confidence in their own correct memories), yet no analysis of these ratings is specified in the analysis plan. This is a reporting/planning gap that also represents undisclosed flexibility.
issues.quote: Moreover, for each question, the participants will be asked to rate the subjective certainty of each answer on a scale from 0% (complete uncertainty, guessing) to 100% (absolute certainty).

issues.subcategory: speculative ranking of intervention efficacy without basis
issues.description: The manuscript predicts a specific efficacy ordering (Demonstration > Extended warning > Education) on largely intuitive grounds, while simultaneously acknowledging substantial content overlap among the three interventions. Predicting a rank order that the design (with overlapping, unmatched interventions) cannot cleanly attribute to specific mechanisms risks confirmation-oriented interpretation.
issues.quote: the Extended warning against misinformation is expected to be slightly less effective than Demonstration and motivation but more effective than Education about memory.

issues.subcategory: stated mechanism (informational influence) not isolable from false-memory mechanism
issues.description: The hypotheses are explicitly tied to the 'informational influence' route and the authors state they do NOT expect effects on false-memory-based conformity. Yet the open-ended/forced-choice individual test cannot distinguish responses driven by genuine false memories from those driven by informational influence (low confidence), so the design cannot test the mechanism-specific predictions the theory makes. The measurement does not map onto the targeted construct.
issues.quote: In this case we do not expect that our proposed methods will make a memory report less contingent on false information provided by a co-witness. Our hypotheses are related mainly to informational influence
